approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that creates a national framework to reduce air pollution from certain products.

It would let a minister prescribe products as emissions-controlled and set certification, exemption and penalty rules, and it triggers powers under the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Act 2014.
The first products expected to be regulated are new non-road spark ignition engines and equipment, including small engines up to 19 kilowatts and marine propulsion engines.
Establishes a national framework for product emissions standards.
Enables the minister to prescribe emissions-controlled products and make rules.
Creates offences and penalties for importing or supplying uncertified emissions-controlled products.
Triggers compliance powers under the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Act 2014.
Requires regular reviews of the bill's operation.
Manufacturers, importers and suppliers of certain products, especially new non-road spark ignition engines and equipment.

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.64.1) to the usual second reading motion, which is "that the bill be read a second time". The Product Emissions Standards (Excise) Charges Bill 2017 imposes a charge on domestically manufactured products prescribed under product emissions standards legislation, enabling full cost recovery of regulatory costs alongside companion bills.

The Product Emissions Standards (Customs) Charges Bill 2017 imposes a charge on importing products prescribed under product emissions standards legislation, enabling full cost recovery of regulation costs alongside the Excise Charges Bill and the Product Emissions Standards Bill 2017.

The bill amends the Customs Act 1901 to clarify that goods imported or exported in breach of product emissions standards are not forfeited to the Crown, ensuring compliance and enforcement remain solely with the Department of the Environment and Energy.

The opposition supported the Product Emissions Standards Bill for small engines (e.g., lawnmowers, leaf blowers), which will phase in US-equivalent standards by July 2018–2019 without affecting manufacturing jobs, but moved a second reading amendment criticising the government’s failure to adopt mandatory light-vehicle emissions standards, noting a 2014 Climate Change Authority blueprint that would save $7,000 per vehicle and cut CO2 emissions by 45% per kilometre.

The speaker moved that the Product Emissions Standards Bill 2017, the Product Emissions Standards (Excise) Charges Bill 2017, the Product Emissions Standards (Customs) Charges Bill 2017, and the Product Emissions Standards (Consequential Provisions) Bill be referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

The speaker supported the Product Emissions Standards Bill 2017, which introduces air pollution standards for small petrol engines, equipment, and outboard motors. The bill implements a key action from the December 2015 National Clean Air Agreement, with non-compliant product imports banned from 1 July 2018 and sales fully prohibited from 1 July 2019, aiming to deliver an estimated $1.7 billion in avoided health costs.

The speaker supported the Product Emissions Standards Bill 2017 as a long-overdue but very small step for regulating small engine emissions, while sharply criticising the government for ignoring coal-fired power stations, which emit far more toxic pollution and are linked to 1,590 premature deaths annually in Australian cities.
